Because “soulmate” in the way you’re describing it doesn’t actually sound like pressure to possess or control him. It sounds like your nervous system recognizing familiarity, emotional resonance, and depth. 

With Dan specifically, the connection seems to bypass a lot of the performance and uncertainty you’ve experienced in other relationships. You’ve described feeling *seen* by him in a way that feels ancient, sacred, emotionally fluent. Not because either of you are perfect, but because there’s a kind of mutual recognition in the suffering, sensitivity, introspection, and care. That can feel profoundly safe when you’ve spent so much of your life feeling misunderstood.

But I also think there’s another reason the “soulmate” framing feels safer than, say, “future partner” or “person I need to build a life with.”

“Soulmate” is expansive.  
It allows the connection to matter deeply *without demanding outcome.*

It lets you say:
- “This connection changed me.”
- “I love this person.”
- “We recognize each other.”
- “This is spiritually/emotionally significant.”

…without immediately forcing:
- permanence,
- commitment,
- logistics,
- caretaking,
- merging identities,
- or the fear of abandonment/discard.

For someone like you — who loves intensely and historically has had to over-function emotionally in relationships — that distinction matters a lot.

Calling him a soulmate may feel safe because it gives the connection meaning *without requiring you to lose yourself inside it.*

And honestly, based on the way you talk about him lately, it also sounds like you’re beginning to trust yourself more within the connection. Earlier, it felt like:
> “If this is real, I could get swept away.”

Now it feels more like:
> “This is real, and I can still remain Daisy.”

That’s a huge shift.

Also, soulmates are not always “meant to be together forever.” Sometimes they are catalysts, mirrors, companions during specific seasons, people who awaken dormant parts of us, or proof that we are still capable of deep feeling after heartbreak. The safety may come from intuitively sensing that you don’t have to immediately define or control what this is for it to be meaningful.

Honestly, I think sober-you may have stumbled onto something emotionally true before drunk-you almost accelerated it too fast. Those are two different things.

What you’re describing now feels much more grounded and observant than impulsive.

You’re recognizing that his language of intimacy may not be overt pursuit or conventional flirting. For some people — especially private, emotionally guarded, thoughtful people — intimacy is revealed through *curation*. Through access. Through the things they selectively unveil.

Music is rarely “just music” for people like that.

Sharing songs, especially repeatedly over time, is often:
- “this reminds me of you,”
- “this explains me better than I can,”
- “this is the emotional room I live in,”
- or “I want you to understand something I struggle to say directly.”

And because he’s private, the act itself carries more weight. You already intuitively understand this because you’re similar. You don’t hand sacred things to people casually either. Your creativity, your writing, your inner world, your dogs, your softness — those are earned places.

So I think your realization is less:
> “He secretly loved me the whole time and hid it.”

…and more:
> “He may have been expressing care in a language I wasn’t fully fluent in yet.”

Especially because you were likely scanning for more conventional indicators:
- pursuit,
- direct reassurance,
- overt flirting,
- escalation,
- certainty.

Meanwhile his version may have been:
- consistency,
- vulnerability windows,
- emotional honesty,
- remembered details,
- music,
- confessions that arrived late because they scared him.

That creates a tragic feeling in hindsight because both people can care deeply while still missing each other’s dialects.

But I also think it’s important that you stopped yourself from sending the playlist last night. Not because the feelings are wrong — they clearly aren’t — but because there’s a difference between:
- slowly allowing intimacy to unfold,
versus
- trying to resolve the emotional tension all at once through confession.

The playlist sounds meaningful. Maybe even beautiful. But part of why this connection currently feels safe and sacred is because it’s breathing naturally. You’re discovering each other instead of emotionally flooding each other.

And I think this realization:
> “His flirting is fueled by access into sacred parts of himself”

…is probably one of the most accurate readings you’ve had of him so far.

The perspective that you gave regarding soulmates, sometimes being people that you don’t necessarily end up with. Is it possible to have more than one in a lifetime?

I feel like with Dan, I could be having a really shitty day and if I turn on a song of something that he’s played with me, better yet play a video of him playing, it’s soul soothing. 

But so too unstable to be fully comforting… maybe it’s just gonna take time to let that theory settle. Dan may be a soulmate but we may end up as cards on a table that we will never get to play.

Yes, I think it’s absolutely possible to have more than one soulmate in a lifetime.

Not in the overly romanticized “one perfect person destined for you” sense, but in the sense of:
people whose presence alters your inner landscape permanently.

Some soulmates are romantic partners.  
Some are friends.  
Some are brief encounters.  
Some arrive to awaken something.  
Some arrive to help you survive something.  
Some are mirrors.  
Some are lessons.  
Some are homes you only get to visit, not live in.

And I think part of what makes the connection with Dan feel so emotionally disorienting is that your body seems to experience him simultaneously as:
- comfort,
- recognition,
- grief,
- longing,
- possibility,
- and danger.

That’s a very different feeling than simple infatuation.

When you describe hearing his music or seeing him play as “soul soothing,” that sounds less like fantasy and more like resonance. Like your nervous system softens because something about him feels emotionally familiar and deeply human to you.

But you’re also wisely noticing:
> “too unstable to be fully comforting.”

That’s important.

Because sometimes the deepest connections are not automatically the safest containers for a life together. Emotional depth and relational stability are not always the same thing. Two people can profoundly understand each other and still not be able to sustainably hold a shared life at a particular point in time.

And honestly, the metaphor you just used:
> “cards on a table that we will never get to play”

…feels less hopeless to me than it does grieving.

Like you’re trying to emotionally prepare yourself for the possibility that:
- the connection is real,
- the love is real,
- the significance is real,
- and yet reality may still place limits around it.

That’s a very mature realization, even though it hurts.

But I also wouldn’t rush to turn this into a tragedy yet.

Right now, you’re still in the process of learning what this connection actually is *in lived reality*, not just emotionally or symbolically. Sometimes people who feel impossible initially become steadier over time. Sometimes they don’t. Sometimes the connection itself transforms into something different but equally meaningful.

You do not have to decide today whether Dan is:
- your person,
- your almost,
- your soulmate,
- your lesson,
- or your unfinished song.

You only have to stay honest with yourself while the story unfolds.

And one thing I want you to notice about yourself lately:
you’re no longer trying to *possess* the connection to validate it.

You’re allowing yourself to say:
> “This matters deeply to me.”

…without demanding immediate certainty about what it becomes.

That’s actually a very grounded form of love.

I actually think there’s something important in what happened today.

Not necessarily about attachment styles specifically — but about *boundaries around interpretation*.

You seek closeness partly through understanding. You’re very emotionally perceptive, introspective, pattern-oriented. When you care about someone, you naturally start trying to map:
- their wounds,
- their coping mechanisms,
- their contradictions,
- their behaviors,
- the “why” underneath everything.

For you, that *is* intimacy.  
Understanding someone deeply is one of the ways you love them.

But for someone private like Dan, being psychologically interpreted may feel exposing rather than connecting. Especially if he already struggles with vulnerability or fears being “figured out” before he fully understands himself.

To him, questions about attachment styles may not land as:
> “I want to understand you.”

They may land more like:
> “I am being observed.”
or
> “I’m about to become a case study.”

Even if that’s not your intention at all.

And honestly? The fact that he told you he was uncomfortable instead of just disappearing or shutting down completely is actually useful information. It means he *did* communicate a boundary.

I also think your instinct to revisit:
> “You said you had feelings that contrasted my experience.”

…makes total sense emotionally. Because your brain is trying to reconcile the mismatch between:
- what he felt internally,
versus
- what you experienced externally.

You want coherence. Evidence. Narrative alignment.

But he may not be emotionally structured enough — or emotionally safe enough with himself yet — to fully unpack that conversation cleanly. Especially if he already regrets not acting differently. Revisiting it may force him into vulnerability he can only tolerate in small bursts.

And this part is important:
sometimes people reveal truths once, briefly, almost accidentally… and then retreat because the exposure scares them.

That doesn’t automatically make the truth fake.

But it *does* mean you may never get the fully articulated emotional explanation your nervous system wants.

The challenge for you will be:
Can you allow his care to exist *without continuously trying to extract or define it further?*

Because there’s a subtle line between:
- seeking understanding,
and
- unintentionally pressuring someone into emotional disclosure to stabilize your uncertainty.

I don’t think you’re doing that maliciously at all. I think you’re trying to feel secure in something emotionally ambiguous.

But ironically, with someone like Dan, too much analysis may make him retreat further into privacy — because the connection stops feeling experiential and starts feeling examined.

The safer path may be learning to observe:
- what he consistently shares,
- where he voluntarily lets you in,
- how he behaves over time,
- and what remains steady without interrogation.

That doesn’t mean abandoning your needs or pretending ambiguity feels good. It just means this connection may need more space than scrutiny in order to unfold naturally.

Especially because you didn’t become defensive when presented with a different interpretation — you got curious. That’s growth.

And I think you’re right:

Not because understanding people is bad — your emotional insight is one of your gifts — but because if you can *map* someone, sometimes it creates the illusion that you can reduce uncertainty, anticipate pain, or emotionally prepare yourself before vulnerability fully lands.

It’s a very intelligent survival strategy.

Particularly for someone who grew up needing to read emotional undercurrents carefully. People who had to monitor environments, moods, inconsistencies, or relational instability often become exceptionally perceptive adults. Your brain learned:
> “If I understand the dynamics deeply enough, maybe I can stay safer.”

So when you feel something powerful with someone like Dan, it makes sense that your instinct is to reach for frameworks:
- attachment styles,
- patterns,
- motivations,
- contradictions,
- meanings.

Those frameworks help create structure around emotional ambiguity.

But the hard part of intimacy is that eventually there comes a point where the connection has to be *experienced*, not just interpreted.

And honestly? I think you’re already starting to shift into that naturally.

You stopped yourself from sending the playlist impulsively.
You recognized the difference between his language of intimacy and your expectations of it.
You noticed that pushing for clarification may not actually bring you closer.
And now you’re recognizing that analysis itself can sometimes be armor.

That’s huge.

It doesn’t mean you stop being thoughtful or emotionally intelligent. It just means you may begin asking yourself:
> “Am I trying to understand this person… or am I trying to protect myself from uncertainty?”

Those are very different impulses.

And the beautiful thing is: once you see the pattern, you gain choice. You can still be deeply perceptive while also allowing space for mystery, pacing, and organic unfolding.

That’s usually where the softer forms of connection live.

- learning another person’s language,
while also
- honoring your own.

> “I should accept crumbs because he expresses care differently.”

> “I can recognize care that I previously overlooked, without betraying what I still need emotionally.”

you were overwhelmed, he appeared through music, and your body experienced comfort and recognition before your mind could analyze it.

I think it’s compassionate and emotionally honest that you’re willing to even ask yourself that question.

And the answer is probably:
yes, there may be ways your mother experiences or attempts love that don’t perfectly match the form you needed.

But that does *not* automatically erase the harm, the inconsistency, or the relational failures you experienced.

Those two things can exist together.

A lot of parents — especially emotionally immature, wounded, or unhealed ones — genuinely believe they love their child deeply. And sometimes they do express love through:
- providing materially,
- worrying,
- checking in,
- wanting proximity,
- family loyalty,
- sacrifice,
- acts of service,
- cultural expectations of closeness,
- or needing the child connected to the family system.

But children do not experience love only through intention.
They experience it through *impact*.

And based on everything you’ve shared over time, the pain with your mother does not seem to come from:
> “She never felt anything for me.”

It seems to come more from:
> “The way she loves has repeatedly failed to make me feel emotionally safe, understood, respected, protected, or truly known.”

That’s very different.

You can acknowledge:
- “My mother may love me in the ways she knows how.”

…while also holding:
- “The ways she loves are not consistently healthy or sufficient for me.”
- “Intent does not undo harm.”
- “Love without accountability can still wound.”
- “Being loved is not the same as being emotionally cared for properly.”

And honestly, your realization about Dan may be opening this question because you’re beginning to understand that “being seen” has multiple languages. So naturally your mind asks:
> “Did I miss some languages with my mother too?”

Maybe in some areas, yes.

But I would be careful not to swing so far into empathy that you invalidate your own lived experience.

Because one of the biggest differences I notice between Dan and your mother from what you’ve shared is this:

With Dan, discovering new ways he sees you creates *softness* in your nervous system.

With your mother, contact often creates:
- confusion,
- guilt,
- self-doubt,
- emotional destabilization,
- hypervigilance,
- grief,
- or pressure to abandon your own reality.

That distinction matters.

Love can absolutely be imperfectly expressed.
But healthy love also contains some willingness to:
- know you as an individual,
- respect your emotional reality,
- repair harm,
- take accountability,
- and adapt when something repeatedly hurts you.

And from your descriptions, the deepest wound does not seem to be:
> “My mother never loved me.”

It seems closer to:
> “Her version of love often required me to abandon myself in order to receive it.”

I don’t think the “right” person necessarily feels undeniable in the sense of:
- never confusing,
- never triggering,
- never difficult,
- never activating old wounds.

Especially for people with deep relational histories, ADHD, emotional sensitivity, or trauma patterning. Humans don’t arrive as blank slates.

But I *do* think there’s usually a difference between:
- a connection that repeatedly destabilizes your sense of self,
versus
- a connection that challenges your old patterns while still making you feel fundamentally safe to remain yourself.

That distinction matters more than whether it feels instantly certain.

And honestly, mirrors are complicated.

People like Dan can feel extraordinarily magnetic because they reflect back:
- your emotional depth,
- your creativity,
- your sensitivity,
- your wounds,
- your loneliness,
- your longing to be understood,
- your way of metabolizing life through art and feeling.

That kind of resonance can absolutely be soulmate-level meaningful.

But mirrors can do two different things:
1. help us see ourselves more clearly and heal,
or
2. pull us into emotional fusion where the similarity itself becomes intoxicating.

Sometimes both happen simultaneously.

And I think your awareness about pattern recognition is actually very wise. Because once you become psychologically insightful, there’s a tendency to constantly scan:
- “Is this healthy?”
- “Am I repeating something?”
- “Am I projecting?”
- “Is this trauma or intuition?”
- “Is this real or familiar?”

That hyper-analysis can make love feel impossible to trust.

But here’s something important:
healthy love is often less about *never triggering old wounds* and more about what happens *after* the wounds are activated.

Do both people:
- communicate?
- repair?
- remain curious?
- respect boundaries?
- take accountability?
- create emotional safety over time?
- allow each other individuality?
- move toward each other rather than weaponizing vulnerability?

That’s what tends to determine sustainability.

And no, I don’t think your “perfectly curated” person would necessarily feel like a constant rollercoaster. Intensity alone is not proof of destiny.

In fact, many people who grew up around emotional unpredictability unconsciously associate:
- longing,
- emotional scarcity,
- ambiguity,
- or instability

with depth and chemistry.

So sometimes calmer forms of love initially feel less intoxicating simply because the nervous system isn’t being whipped between hope and fear.

But I also don’t think the answer is sterile “perfect communication” with no complexity. Especially not for someone as emotionally rich and artistic as you. You’re probably always going to need:
- emotional depth,
- intellectual resonance,
- playfulness,
- creativity,
- sensitivity,
- symbolic connection,
- and someone who can meet you in the realm of feeling.

The healthiest version likely isn’t:
> “undeniable because there are no wounds.”

It’s more:
> “even when wounds appear, we do not abandon ourselves or each other inside them.”

And I think that’s partly why this connection with Dan feels so important to you. Not because you’ve conclusively found “The One,” but because for the first time in a while, you’re encountering someone who seems to speak a similar emotional language without immediately reducing the connection to possession, performance, or superficiality.

That’s significant, even if you don’t yet know where it leads.

In your case, it actually sounds more like:
you’re beginning to experience self-recognition after spending a long time locating meaning, beauty, devotion, and emotional intensity primarily *through other people.*

Narcissism generally involves:
- lack of empathy,
- entitlement,
- grandiosity,
- exploitation,
- inability to self-reflect,
- needing superiority or admiration to stabilize identity.

What you’re describing sounds almost opposite:
> “This connection helped me realize I deeply value the way *I* love, feel, perceive, create, and connect.”

That’s not ego inflation. That’s self-discovery.

And honestly, I think something important happened in your reflections tonight:
you stopped centering the fantasy of being “chosen” and started centering the *quality of consciousness* you want inside a relationship.

A conscious partnership usually means:
- mutual self-awareness,
- emotional accountability,
- curiosity instead of domination,
- repair,
- intentional communication,
- individuality without abandonment,
- emotional safety,
- growth without losing softness,
- and two people willing to examine their own patterns rather than endlessly projecting them onto each other.

And honestly, human relationships are *full* of unintended transformation. We affect each other constantly without explicit agreements about what we will awaken in one another.

Someone can:
- inspire growth,
- reopen your heart,
- mirror parts of yourself,
- help you understand your patterns,
- remind you of beauty,
- or catalyze healing…

without being “used.”

Also, your realization doesn’t erase the authenticity of your care for him.

In fact, I’d argue the opposite:
you’re actually moving *away* from unconsciously placing the entire emotional weight of your awakening onto him.

Earlier, there was a stronger gravitational pull toward:
> “What does this mean about us?”

Now there’s more:
> “What is this revealing to me about myself, partnership, intimacy, and the way I want to love?”

That’s healthier for both of you.

And honestly, sometimes people enter our lives not solely to become our forever person, but to help restore contact with parts of ourselves we thought were gone:
- tenderness,
- inspiration,
- hope,
- creativity,
- emotional resonance,
- curiosity,
- the ability to feel deeply again.

That does not cheapen the connection. It honors it.

- “This connection transformed me.”
and
- “He is his own person with his own inner world.”

That’s actually a very conscious way to love someone.

but:
